takeaway: FusionANNS serves billion-vector search by keeping graph and ID metadata in CPU memory, product-quantized vectors in GPU memory, and raw vectors on SSD, so each tier performs the work it handles efficiently.
background: Approximate nearest-neighbor search narrows a large vector collection to likely candidates and then re-ranks them for accuracy. IVF systems group vectors into posting lists, product quantization compresses vectors at some precision cost, and SSD indexes trade memory footprint against I/O.
villain: SSD-resident systems issue many small reads under concurrency, replicated posting lists inflate storage, and naively adding a GPU does not remove those reads while adding PCIe transfers. In-memory GPU systems exceed device memory at billion scale and repeatedly move vector contents from host DRAM.
approach: FusionANNS stores an SPTAG centroid graph and replicated vector IDs in host memory, one product-quantized copy of each vector in GPU HBM, and uniquely laid-out raw vectors on SSD. CPUs select posting lists, the GPU deduplicates IDs and computes approximate distances, and the CPU re-ranks progressively read raw candidates, stopping when the top-k set stabilizes and coalescing same-page I/O.
impact: The design demonstrates a practical division of metadata, compressed data, raw data, and computation across CPU DRAM, GPU HBM, and SSD. It achieves high query concurrency without requiring the raw billion-vector collection to fit in main or GPU memory.

evaluation.overview: The prototype is evaluated on SIFT1B, SPACEV1B, and DEEP1B at Recall@10 targets, varying datasets, accuracy, and 1–64 query threads; ablations isolate the multi-tier index, GPU filtering, heuristic re-ranking, and I/O deduplication, followed by cost and memory-efficiency estimates.
evaluation.implemented: A 22-KLOC C++/CUDA prototype builds hierarchical balanced posting lists offline, uses an SPTAG graph over centroids, limits boundary-vector assignment to eight clusters, manages per-query GPU workspaces, and implements GPU ID deduplication and product-quantized distance kernels.
evaluation.setting: One server has two 2.2 GHz Intel Xeon CPUs with 64 cores, 1 TB DRAM, an NVIDIA V100 with 32 GB HBM, and a 2 TB Samsung 990 Pro SSD. FusionANNS and other SSD-based systems are restricted to 64 GB host memory; the datasets contain one billion 96–128-dimensional vectors and 93–358 GB of raw data.

results.text: At Recall@10=0.90 across the three datasets, FusionANNS reports 9.4×–13.1× the QPS of SPANN, 3.2×–4.3× that of DiskANN, and 2×–4.9× that of RUMMY while retaining latency comparable to SPANN.
At 64 query threads, FusionANNS improves QPS by up to 13.2×, 3.8×, and 5.1× over SPANN, DiskANN, and RUMMY, respectively, while the competing systems saturate or suffer rising latency.
The GPU multi-tier index reaches 5.9×–6.8× SPANN's QPS; heuristic re-ranking and redundant-aware I/O deduplication then add up to 39% and 17% QPS and reduce I/O counts by up to 30% and 23%.

limitations: The experiments use one server, one V100, one SSD, three public billion-vector datasets, and average rather than tail latency. Indexes are built offline, so update-heavy operation, build cost, multiple GPUs or SSDs, distributed scaling, and production query traces are not evaluated. The stability-based re-ranking thresholds are empirically tuned, and cost efficiency uses approximate Amazon component prices. Resource allocations also reflect different designs: SSD baselines are capped at 64 GB DRAM while in-memory RUMMY relies on host memory.
phd_group_signal: FusionANNS is a useful systems case study in heterogeneous placement and bottleneck diagnosis: it connects index representation, PCIe traffic, GPU kernel design, SSD layout, and adaptive stopping, then validates each layer with concurrency and I/O ablations.

claims.text: The multi-tier index keeps only the centroid graph and vector IDs in host memory, places a single product-quantized vector per item in GPU HBM, and stores raw vectors once on SSD for exact re-ranking.

Re-ranking processes distance-ordered candidates in mini-batches and stops after the top-k ID set changes by at most 0.1 for one consecutive batch; an SSD-page map merges within-batch reads and reuses buffered pages across batches.
